parts.title: The Origins of Weather Forecasting
parts.subtitle: The world’s first public weather forecast appeared in The Times newspaper over 150 years ago: the beginning of a service that gives everyone something to comment on
parts.article:
The Origins of Weather Forecasting

(A) The pioneering forecast on August 1, 1861, was introduced with a deceptively simple heading: ‘General weather probable during next two days.’ But those few words started an ongoing controversy that still continues today - after all, everyone remembers the forecasts that go wrong, but rarely the ones that are right.

(B) The first forecast was the idea of Admiral Robert FitzRoy, head of the newly founded Meteorological Department, and one of Britain’s greatest but least-known heroes. It was a brave undertaking, because in those days predicting the weather had gained a reputation similar to astrology or fortune-telling. The few people who attempted it had become a national joke when their forecasts inevitably went wrong.

(C) FitzRoy was different, though. His background was faultless, most famously his captaining of the ship HMS Beagle on Charles Darwin’s voyage around the world, which eventually led to the publication of Darwin’s well-known book On the Origin of Species. When FitzRoy retired from active service as an admiral in Britain’s navy, he was looking for a new direction. He subsequently secured a job as chief statistician at the Meteorological Department, part of the Board of Trade. Parliament had voted to set up and fund the Meteorological Department on June 30, 1854, to chart the safest sailing routes across the Atlantic Ocean. However, the British Government was not impressed with the idea of collecting weather reports and establishing a weather forecast, and the suggestion by one Member of Parliament for this was met with laughter from the other MPs.

(D) FitzRoy was given a staff of three clerks in a small office in London, but he soon grew bored with the tedium of transcribing thousands of ships’ reports. Instead, he focused on a much more pressing issue - the huge loss of life at sea from storms. This problem came to a head in 1859, when gale-force winds sank the ship named Royal Charter, with the loss of 430 lives, within sight of the shore. Even in those days when ships regularly sank in storms, the loss of the Royal Charter was considered a national tragedy. FitzRoy stirred up feelings even further when he wrote a letter to The Times newspaper explaining that the storm had been entirely predictable.

(E) That same year, a total of 1,645 lives were lost off the British coast, and FitzRoy wrote repeatedly to The Times pushing for a storm-warning service for shipping. This was just the right moment for a national forecasting service. Knowledge of the weather was improving, barometer readings gave warning of approaching storms, and the invention of the electric telegraph and Morse code in 1844 gave instant communication for the first time.

(F) So in February 1861, FitzRoy pressed ahead with a storm-warning service. Previously, weather reports had been unreliable, but FitzRoy’s innovation was to issue ships with standardised instruments which allowed for accurate weather reports. At exactly the same time each day the information was sent to him by telegraph, and he was able to draw up more detailed weather maps. The approach of an incoming storm could be recognised, and from London, FitzRoy could telegraph warnings to ports on the coast, where an ingenious system of flags was hoisted up high for passing ships to read. This represented the biggest advance in shipping safety after the introduction of the lifeboat, and in subsequent years the number of lives lost around Britain fell by about a third. FitzRoy became a hero to the fishing and maritime fleets.

(G) Encouraged by his storm-warning success, FitzRoy then started a public weather forecasting service. As he had a close connection with The Times, this newspaper introduced his daily forecast in August 1861. It attracted huge attention, including from Queen Victoria, who regularly sent messengers to FitzRoy’s office to get a forecast for the sea crossing over the Solent to an island which she liked to visit off the south coast of England. He was also popular with ordinary fishermen, who were happy not to be out at sea in bad weather. The owners of fishing vessels, however, were not supportive of FitzRoy’s forecasts, which often caused delays for them when bad weather was forecast.

(H) Nevertheless, weather forecasting at that time was very difficult, and one mistake could result in much bad publicity. It wasn’t long before some forecasts turned out wrong, and the letters pages of The Times were full of heated correspondence. It is indisputable that FitzRoy was way ahead of his time, but it is only in recent years that he has been recognised as a towering figure in meteorology, with the honour of an area of sea being given his name in the shipping forecast (a radio broadcast of weather reports for the seas around Britain). His extraordinary determination to get forecasting established cost him dearly though, and he died prematurely. But his legacy lives on, because late in his life he published a book about weather forecasting which was recognised by other scientists to be well ahead of its time.

questions.question: In Robert FitzRoy’s time, weather forecasting was a respected skill.

analyses.content: 原文说当时预测天气名声不好，像占星术算命一样，甚至成了全国的笑话，说明这并非受人尊敬的技能。
你可能只看到了“predicting the weather”，但没注意到后面的贬义词“astrology”（占星术）和“national joke”（全国的笑话），从而误以为天气预报当时很受尊敬。

It was a brave undertaking, because in those days predicting the weather had gained a reputation similar to astrology or fortune-telling. The few people who attempted it had become a national joke when their forecasts inevitably went wrong.

questions.question: When FitzRoy retired from the navy, he had already had a successful career at sea.

analyses.content: 原文明确提到他退役前有着无可挑剔的背景，特别是担任了著名舰船（HMS Beagle）的船长，说明他的航海生涯非常成功。
你可能不认识“faultless”（完美无瑕的）这个词，从而无法判断他退役前的事业是否成功。

His background was faultless, most famously his captaining of the ship HMS Beagle on Charles Darwin’s voyage around the world, which eventually led to the publication of Darwin’s well-known book On the Origin of Species. When FitzRoy retired from active service as an admiral in Britain’s navy, he was looking for a new direction.

questions.question: FitzRoy faced competition from other applicants for the chief statistician’s job.

analyses.content: 原文只提到他获得了首席统计员（chief statistician）这份工作，完全没有提及是否有其他申请人与他竞争。
你可能脑补了他找工作一定有竞争对手，但做阅读判断题千万不能用常理推测，原文没写就是没写。
He subsequently secured a job as chief statistician at the Meteorological Department, part of the Board of Trade.

questions.question: The British Parliament supported the idea of regular weather forecasts in 1854.

analyses.content: 原文明确指出英国政府对收集天气报告和建立天气预报的想法不感兴趣，甚至有议员的建议还遭到了其他人的嘲笑，说明议会并不支持。
你可能只看到1854年议会出钱成立了气象部门，就误以为他们支持天气预报，但实际上他们当时的目的是规划航线，并且紧接着的句子明确表达了他们对天气预报的嘲笑与不支持。

Parliament had voted to set up and fund the Meteorological Department on June 30, 1854, to chart the safest sailing routes across the Atlantic Ocean. However, the British Government was not impressed with the idea of collecting weather reports and establishing a weather forecast, and the suggestion by one Member of Parliament for this was met with laughter from the other MPs.

questions.question: Progress in technology made it a good time for publicly available weather forecasting to begin.

analyses.content: 原文提到当时正是建立国家预报服务的好时机，紧接着解释了这是因为电报机和摩斯密码的出现提供了即时通讯，这完全对应了题目中技术进步带来了好时机的说法。
你可能没有把原文中具体的“the invention of the electric telegraph”（电报的发明）抽象概括为题目里的“Progress in technology”（技术进步），导致无法确认对应关系。

This was just the right moment for a national forecasting service. Knowledge of the weather was improving, barometer readings gave warning of approaching storms, and the invention of the electric telegraph and Morse code in 1844 gave instant communication for the first time.

analyses.content: 题目问船只使用什么可靠的东西来生成天气报告，原文明确提到给船只发放了标准化的仪器（instruments）以实现准确的天气报告。
你可能会错误地想填“reports”，但题目问的是使用什么工具来生成reports，必须往后看找到用来操作的具体物品“instruments”。
Previously, weather reports had been unreliable, but FitzRoy’s innovation was to issue ships with standardised instruments which allowed for accurate weather reports.
题目问风暴警告被电报发送到了海岸沿线的什么地方，原文直接说用电报发送警告给海岸上的港口（ports）。
你可能看到“coast”就觉得是答案，但题目中已经有了“along the shore”（沿着海岸，对应原文on the coast），所以你要填的是具体的地点词“ports”。

The approach of an incoming storm could be recognised, and from London, FitzRoy could telegraph warnings to ports on the coast, where an ingenious system of flags was hoisted up high for passing ships to read.
题目问给船只的信号是使用升起的什么来展示的，原文说一套巧妙的旗帜（flags）被高高升起供路过的船只阅读。
你可能不认识“hoisted”（升起）这个词，导致无法将其与题目中的“raised”对应上，从��找不到它修饰的核心名词“flags”。

The approach of an incoming storm could be recognised, and from London, FitzRoy could telegraph warnings to ports on the coast, where an ingenious system of flags was hoisted up high for passing ships to read.
题目问这是自什么被引入以来海上安全最大的发展，原文直接对应说这是继救生艇（lifeboat）引入之后最大的进步。
你可能会去原文寻找“greatest development”的原词，但原文将其同义替换成了“biggest advance”，如果没有识别出这个替换就会错过答案。
This represented the biggest advance in shipping safety after the introduction of the lifeboat, and in subsequent years the number of lives lost around Britain fell by about a third.
题目问英国女王经常为了安全前往一个最喜欢的什么地方而使用预报，原文明确提到女王获取预报是为了去一个她喜欢游览的岛屿（island）。
你可能会被“Solent”这个专有名词干扰而填错，但题目需要填写的是女王喜欢去的目的地，结合原文“an island which she liked to visit”，答案只能是island。

It attracted huge attention, including from Queen Victoria, who regularly sent messengers to FitzRoy’s office to get a forecast for the sea crossing over the Solent to an island which she liked to visit off the south coast of England.
题目问预报受渔民欢迎，但不受哪种船只相关的人欢迎，原文直接点出渔船的所有者（owners）并不支持他的预报。
你可能只看到了“vessels”（船只），但没有注意到题目中已经有了同义词“boat”，所以你需要填的是人，即“owners”。

He was also popular with ordinary fishermen, who were happy not to be out at sea in bad weather. The owners of fishing vessels, however, were not supportive of FitzRoy’s forecasts, which often caused delays for them when bad weather was forecast.
题目问在现代FitzRoy的什么被用于一个海域，原文说近年来作为一种荣誉，一个海域被赋予了他的名字（name）。
你可能会因为长难句而迷失，没有抓住“area of sea”和“given his name”之间的直接对应关系，导致找不到答案。

It is indisputable that FitzRoy was way ahead of his time, but it is only in recent years that he has been recognised as a towering figure in meteorology, with the honour of an area of sea being given his name in the shipping forecast (a radio broadcast of weather reports for the seas around Britain).
题目问他制作了一个受科学界尊敬的什么，原文直接提到他出版了一本书（book），并且这本书被其他科学家高度认可。
你可能会想填“forecast”，但原文明确说明受到其他科学家认可（对应题目respected by the scientific community）的是他晚年出版的“book”。
But his legacy lives on, because late in his life he published a book about weather forecasting which was recognised by other scientists to be well ahead of its time.
